summary: Adjunct antiseizure medication for Dravet syndrome—used with clobazam (and often valproate internationally). Not a psychiatric medication, but it can strongly affect sleep, energy, behavior, and sedation.
description: Diacomit (stiripentol) is an add-on seizure medication for Dravet syndrome. In the U.S., it’s approved with clobazam—not as monotherapy. International guidance commonly uses it with both clobazam and valproic acid. It can cause heavy drowsiness, agitation, insomnia, and appetite/weight loss, and it has major drug interaction potential because it inhibits multiple liver enzymes. If you’re switching between capsules and powder, your exposure can change—so monitoring matters.
patient_summary: Diacomit (stiripentol) is an add-on seizure medication for Dravet syndrome. It’s not a psychiatric med, but it can seriously impact sedation, sleep, agitation, appetite, and mood. It’s used with clobazam (and often valproate internationally), and it has big interaction risk—so med list reviews and monitoring aren’t optional.

primary.context: Used as adjunct therapy for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome. In the U.S., it’s FDA-approved in combination with clobazam; international labeling commonly recommends combination with clobazam and valproic acid. Not appropriate for monotherapy.

secondary.context: Not indicated to treat insomnia. Sleep changes (including insomnia or sedation) are side effects, not treatment targets.
Not indicated to treat agitation. Agitation and aggressive behavior can occur as adverse effects and should prompt reassessment.

common_adverse_effects.notes: This can feel like a heavy blanket over the day—slower thinking, less energy, more naps. If it’s interfering with functioning, clinicians often reassess clobazam dosing (and other sedating meds) because interactions can amplify sedation.
Agitation can show up as restlessness, irritability, or a shorter fuse. If agitation increases after starting or titrating, it deserves a full medication review—not just “wait it out.”
Unsteady gait and clumsiness increase fall risk. This matters even more if sedation is also present.
Lower muscle tone can look like “floppier” posture or less physical stability—often alongside fatigue/sedation.
Sleep can get disrupted in either direction—some get sleepy, others get wired or wakeful. Track sleep patterns because it helps guide adjustments.
Loss of appetite can be a big deal, especially in kids. Weight trends matter more than a single day of picky eating—monitor consistently.
Weight loss can follow appetite suppression. If weight drops or growth slows, the regimen may need adjustment.
GI side effects can worsen appetite and weight loss—treating nausea and timing with meals may help.
Tremor can be subtle or obvious and may interfere with fine motor tasks; it can also overlap with other antiseizure meds’ side effects.
Low platelets can increase bruising/bleeding risk. This is why CBC monitoring isn’t optional.
Low neutrophils can increase infection risk. If fevers or recurrent infections occur, labs should be checked promptly.

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal thoughts/behavior warning (antiseizure medication class): Monitor for new or worsening depression, unusual behavior changes, or self-harm thoughts
Clinically significant blood dyscrasias (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia): Requires CBC monitoring and clinical correlation
Severe sedation/CNS depression with impaired functioning: Particularly relevant when combined with clobazam and other sedating medications
Worsening seizure control if stopped abruptly: Increased seizure frequency and risk of status epilepticus

contraindications.contraindication: None listed in U.S. manufacturer labeling
Canadian labeling: Hypersensitivity to stiripentol or any component of the formulation

precautions: Appropriate use: Not for monotherapy. In the U.S., approved as adjunct treatment with clobazam; international guidance often recommends use with both clobazam and valproic acid
CNS depression: Can cause significant drowsiness and impair alertness; caution with driving or hazardous activities when applicable
Suicidal ideation/behavior warning (antiseizure medication class): Increased risk has been observed across antiseizure medications; monitor for mood/behavior changes
Blood dyscrasias: Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia have been reported; CBC monitoring is recommended
Appetite/weight loss: Can be clinically significant—especially in children; monitor growth and weight closely
Renal/hepatic impairment: Not studied for dose adjustments; avoid in moderate to severe renal or hepatic impairment; use caution and titrate carefully in mild impairment
Powder contains phenylalanine (aspartame): Use caution in phenylketonuria
Hazardous handling considerations: May meet criteria for hazardous drugs; use appropriate precautions per institutional policy

interactions.mechanism: Sedation and CNS depression can increase due to interaction-driven higher exposure to clobazam and/or active metabolites.
interactions.action: Monitor closely for excessive drowsiness, slowed cognition, or functional impairment. Dose adjustment of clobazam may be needed when stiripentol is initiated or titrated.

interactions.mechanism: International regimens commonly include valproate; appetite/weight loss and sedation may worsen depending on the full combination.
interactions.action: Monitor appetite, weight, and overall tolerability. In some regimens, clinicians consider valproate dose reduction to help minimize appetite/weight loss.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (including sedating antihistamines, sleep meds, alcohol, cannabis products)
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation, impaired coordination, increased fall risk, and worse cognitive slowing.
interactions.action: Avoid stacking sedatives when possible. If unavoidable, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely.

interactions.interactant: Medications metabolized by CYP1A2, CYP2C19, CYP3A4
interactions.mechanism: Stiripentol inhibits CYP1A2 (moderate), CYP2C19 (moderate), and CYP3A4 (weak), which can raise levels of co-medications and increase side effects.
interactions.action: Do a full medication reconciliation and interaction review whenever starting, stopping, or changing stiripentol dose. Adjust companion drug doses as needed based on clinical response and side effects.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: CBC: Prior to initiation and every 6 months (or as clinically indicated) due to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia risk
Weight and appetite: Track weight trends; in children, monitor growth rate closely
Sedation and functioning: Watch for excessive drowsiness, slowed cognition, and impaired coordination—especially in combination with clobazam and other sedating meds
Behavior and mood: Monitor for agitation, aggression, irritability, insomnia, and any new or worsening depression or suicidal thoughts/behavior
Medication interactions: Re-check the full medication list whenever doses change or when switching formulations (capsule ↔ powder) because exposure and companion-drug levels can shift
Formulation switches: Systemic exposure may be slightly higher with powder for suspension than capsules; monitor clinically when switching
PKU considerations: Powder for suspension contains phenylalanine (aspartame); use caution and monitor as appropriate

special_populations.pregnancy: Outcome data are limited and insufficient to define specific risks for major congenital malformations or neurodevelopmental outcomes with stiripentol exposure. Epilepsy management during pregnancy should use shared decision-making to optimize seizure control and plan for pregnancy when possible. Patients should be encouraged to enroll in the North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if stiripentol is present in breast milk. The decision to breastfeed should consider potential infant exposure, benefits of breastfeeding, and benefits of treatment to the parent. If breastfeeding occurs while on antiseizure meds, monitor the infant for sedation, poor sucking, weight gain issues, abnormal platelet counts, abnormal liver function, and developmental milestones.
special_populations.pediatric: FDA-labeled for adjunctive treatment of Dravet syndrome seizures in patients ≥6 months of age and weighing ≥7 kg (with clobazam). Psychiatric relevance in pediatrics is mainly side effects: sedation, agitation/aggression, sleep disruption, and appetite/weight impacts that can affect development and daily functioning.
special_populations.geriatric: Refer to adult dosing. Not applicable for this medication in typical practice, as Dravet syndrome is primarily pediatric-onset; if used in older patients, titrate cautiously due to sedation and interaction risk.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No manufacturer-provided dose adjustments (not studied). Use caution in mild impairment and titrate based on seizure control and tolerability; avoid use in moderate to severe renal impairment.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No manufacturer-provided dose adjustments (not studied). Use caution in mild impairment and titrate based on seizure control and tolerability; avoid use in moderate to severe hepatic impairment.

pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults: ~4.5 to 13 hours (dose-dependent); pediatric half-life increases with body weight in modeling studies
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via demethylenation (CYP1A2, CYP2C19, CYP3A4) and glucuronidation
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (~73% as metabolites); feces (~18% unchanged drug)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Administer with meals/food; powder may produce slightly higher systemic exposure than capsules

dosing.titration: Diacomit dosing is weight-based and designed for seizure control in Dravet syndrome as adjunct therapy (not monotherapy). There are no psychiatric dosing indications for this medication.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Stiripentol isn’t a psychiatric medication, but stopping it abruptly can still be dangerous—because seizure medications should generally be withdrawn gradually to avoid rebound seizure worsening and status epilepticus. If urgent safety concerns exist, the prescriber will weigh a faster change against seizure risk.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Diacomit (stiripentol) is not a psychiatric medication. Its approved role is seizure control in Dravet syndrome—and even then, it’s meant to be used as add-on therapy, not solo. Psychiatry becomes relevant because this med can hit the brain hard: sedation, sleep disruption, agitation, appetite/weight loss, and a class-wide warning about suicidal thoughts/behavior.
items: {link:condition:dravet-syndrome:Dravet syndrome–associated seizures}: Adjunctive therapy (U.S.: with clobazam; international guidance often includes valproic acid too)
Not for monotherapy: Clinical trial data are limited to combination use (especially with clobazam + valproate in key studies)

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It helped seizures, but the sleepiness was intense.
My kid looked wiped out—like the day got quieter and slower.
We had to rethink the whole schedule because mornings were rough.
items.note: Drowsiness is very common, especially alongside clobazam. If sedation becomes a problem, clinicians often reassess clobazam (and sometimes other antiseizure meds) because interactions can raise exposure.

quotes: It was weird—sleepy, but also more irritable.
We saw more agitation than usual and it got our attention fast.
items.note: Agitation and aggressive behavior have been reported. New or escalating behavioral symptoms should trigger a medication review (including interaction-driven overexposure).

quotes: I expected sedation, but sleep got choppy.
Falling asleep was easier, staying asleep wasn’t.
items.note: Insomnia is reported in some patients even though sedation is also common. Sleep changes can go in either direction.

quotes: Appetite dropped hard—like food just wasn’t appealing.
We had to track weight because it started sliding.
items.note: Decreased appetite and weight loss are common and need proactive monitoring—especially in children. Dose adjustments of valproate may be considered in some regimens to help minimize appetite/weight loss.

sections.intro: This medication isn’t prescribed for mood or anxiety—but it can absolutely change how someone feels day to day. These are the psychiatry-relevant patterns people commonly report when sedation, sleep, appetite, and behavior shift on stiripentol-based regimens:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: For psychiatry-relevant effects, the timeline is mostly about sedation, sleep, and behavior changes—not rapid symptom relief like a PRN anxiety med.
key_points: 2-3 hours: Blood levels typically peak after a dose
First days to weeks: Sedation, sleep changes, appetite changes, and irritability can show up early and may shift as doses are titrated
4.5-13 hours: Adult elimination half-life (dose-dependent), meaning effects can accumulate with repeated dosing
Formulation switch matters: Powder for suspension can produce slightly higher exposure than capsules—monitor closely when switching

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Stiripentol isn’t used to treat psychiatric conditions like anxiety, panic, or insomnia. Its benefits are measured in seizure control for Dravet syndrome. From a psychiatry lens, the “efficacy” conversation is really about tolerability—how sedation, sleep disruption, appetite/weight loss, and behavioral changes impact quality of life and day-to-day functioning.
sections.clinical_details: Clinical trial experience is largely in patients receiving stiripentol alongside clobazam and valproic acid, and real-world regimens may require adjustment of those companion medications because stiripentol can increase exposure via enzyme inhibition. When psychiatric or behavioral side effects show up, the fix is often a regimen-level adjustment—not just blaming one medication.

Track appetite and weight, especially in kids. If eating drops off, bring it up early—don’t wait for a growth dip.
Report new depression, self-harm thoughts, or unusual behavior changes right away.
If switching between capsules and powder, monitor closely—exposure can change.

sections.intro: Stiripentol is an interaction-heavy medication. It inhibits multiple CYP enzymes and can raise levels of other drugs—especially relevant when the regimen includes clobazam (and often valproate). From a psychiatry perspective, interaction-driven over-sedation or behavior changes are the red flags.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stiripentol isn’t a psychiatric medication, but stopping it abruptly can still be dangerous—because seizure medications should generally be withdrawn gradually to avoid rebound seizure worsening and status epilepticus. If urgent safety concerns exist, the prescriber will weigh a faster change against seizure risk.
key_points: Do not stop abruptly unless a clinician directs it for a safety emergency
With chronic therapy, withdraw gradually to minimize increased seizure frequency and risk of status epilepticus
When tapering, the entire regimen matters (stiripentol + clobazam ± valproate and others): changes can shift sedation, sleep, and behavior as drug levels rebalance
If behavioral symptoms (agitation, insomnia) worsen during a change, notify the care team—this may reflect interaction shifts rather than a “new psychiatric problem”

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Diacomit dosing is weight-based and designed for seizure control in Dravet syndrome as adjunct therapy (not monotherapy). There are no psychiatric dosing indications for this medication.
sections.simple_explanation: This is a seizure medication used in combination regimens (commonly with clobazam, and often with valproate internationally). Because it strongly affects drug metabolism and can increase exposure to other meds, dosing and tolerability are managed as a full-regimen problem—not a single-drug problem.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Stiripentol isn’t a psychiatric medication, but pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions still matter because seizure control is high-stakes and medication exposures can affect both parent and baby. Data on stiripentol in pregnancy are limited. When used, it’s usually part of a combination regimen—so risk/benefit decisions involve the whole plan (including clobazam and valproate).
sections.pregnancy: Outcome data are limited and insufficient to define specific risks for major congenital malformations or neurodevelopmental outcomes with stiripentol exposure. Epilepsy management during pregnancy should use shared decision-making to optimize seizure control and plan for pregnancy when possible. Patients should be encouraged to enroll in the North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry.
sections.lactation: It is not known if stiripentol is present in breast milk. The decision to breastfeed should consider potential infant exposure, benefits of breastfeeding, and benefits of treatment to the parent. If breastfeeding occurs while on antiseizure meds, monitor the infant for sedation, poor sucking, weight gain issues, abnormal platelet counts, abnormal liver function, and developmental milestones.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Diacomit comes as capsules and powder packets for oral suspension. Switching forms can change drug exposure, so it’s not a casual swap—monitor when transitioning.
items: Powder packets for suspension: 250 mg, 500 mg (oral; contains aspartame/phenylalanine)
Administration: Take with meals/food; capsules should be swallowed whole; powder packets are mixed with water and consumed immediately

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: The exact antiseizure mechanism isn’t fully defined. Stiripentol may enhance inhibitory GABA signaling (including effects at GABA-A receptors). It also inhibits multiple CYP enzymes, which can increase systemic exposure to other antiseizure medications—this is a major reason interaction management is central to safe use.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Diacomit is a specialized add-on medication for Dravet syndrome seizures, typically used in combination with clobazam (and often valproate internationally). From a psychiatry perspective, the key clinical issue is not “using it for mood,” but managing neurobehavioral and sleep side effects that can mimic or worsen psychiatric symptoms—especially when interaction effects push companion drug levels higher.

faqs.a: No. Diacomit is a seizure medication used for Dravet syndrome as add-on therapy. Psychiatry still matters because it can affect sedation, sleep, appetite, and behavior—and it has a class warning about suicidal thoughts/behavior.

Diacomit is used as adjunctive treatment for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome. In the U.S., it’s approved in combination with clobazam for patients ≥6 months old who weigh ≥7 kg. It’s not meant to be used as monotherapy.

faqs.q: Why do people get so sleepy on stiripentol?
faqs.a: Drowsiness is very common with stiripentol-based regimens, especially because it’s used with clobazam. Stiripentol also inhibits liver enzymes that metabolize other medications, which can increase exposure and worsen sedation. If sleepiness becomes excessive, the prescriber may adjust clobazam or other parts of the regimen.

faqs.q: Can Diacomit cause agitation or behavior problems?
faqs.a: Yes. Agitation and aggressive behavior have been reported. If behavior noticeably worsens after starting or increasing the dose, it deserves a prompt medication review—especially to check for interaction-driven overexposure.

faqs.q: Can Diacomit cause insomnia even if it also causes drowsiness?
faqs.a: Yes. Both can happen. Some people experience heavy sedation, while others have insomnia or fragmented sleep. Tracking sleep patterns is useful because it helps guide regimen adjustments.

faqs.q: What are the biggest monitoring priorities from a psychiatry perspective?
faqs.a: Watch sedation and day-to-day functioning, sleep changes (insomnia or oversedation), appetite/weight loss, irritability/agitation, and mood shifts including any suicidal thoughts. Because interactions are central with this medication, monitoring also includes frequent medication list reviews.

faqs.q: Are there lab tests needed with stiripentol?
faqs.a: Yes. CBC monitoring is recommended because neutropenia and thrombocytopenia have been observed. Weight and growth monitoring are also important in pediatric patients.

faqs.q: What should I know about switching between capsules and powder?
faqs.a: Systemic exposure can be slightly higher with the powder for suspension compared with capsules. So switching forms can change effects and side effects. When a switch happens, monitoring should increase—especially for sedation, appetite, and behavior changes.

faqs.q: Is Diacomit safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Pregnancy data are limited, and it’s not known if stiripentol is present in breast milk. Decisions should weigh seizure control needs and potential fetal/infant exposure, and they should consider the full combination regimen (including clobazam and valproate when used). Enrollment in the NAAED Pregnancy Registry is encouraged.

faqs.q: Can I stop stiripentol suddenly if side effects are bad?
faqs.a: Don’t stop abruptly unless a clinician directs it for an urgent safety reason. Sudden discontinuation of antiseizure medications can increase seizure frequency and raise the risk of status epilepticus. If side effects feel severe, contact the prescriber quickly to adjust the plan safely.
